Paragraph:
Travelling deeper into the forest the exiles beheld the unsurpassed beauties of nature, which were mesmeric. At sunset they reached the confluence of the rivers Ganga and Yamuna where at a distance rose a column of smoke. Knowing it to be the region where the hermitage of Bharadhvaja was situated and walking towards it they saw the sage finishing his evening worship. Bowing to him Rama said, 'We are the sons of Dasaratha, Rama and Lakshmana and this is my consort Sita. I am here banished from Ayodhya, commanded by my father to lead the life of an ascetic.'

Bharadhvaja welcomed and honored the guests with his impeccable hospitality telling them that he knew of the advent of Rama. He said that the place they were now in, was at the confluence of two sacred rivers and most suitable for their ascetic pursuits. But Rama said, 'This wonderful place is too close to Ayodhya and my people will be tempted to visit us often. So I wish to move on to a region less accessible.'The sage then suggested that ten miles from his hermitage was the mountain Chitrakuta. There innumerable ascetics had performed rigorous penance, attaining heaven with their mortal bodies. Rama gratefully thanked Bharadhvaja for the information and passed that night at the hermitage.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Rama and his companions are journeying into exile, seeking a suitable place for their ascetic life. Rama consciously chooses a location that is further removed from Ayodhya to prevent his grieving subjects from frequently visiting him, which he believes would hinder both their ability to move on and his own commitment to exile.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Rama demonstrates clear emotional regulation and a proactive approach to stress management. He acknowledges the potential for continued emotional distress if he stays too close to Ayodhya and makes a pragmatic decision to move deeper into the forest. This decision prioritizes the long-term goal of his exile and the well-being of his people.
Outcome/Resolution: Rama gratefully accepts Bharadhvaja's suggestion of Chitrakuta, a more remote location. They spend the night at the hermitage, preparing to move to a place more conducive to their ascetic vows and less disruptive to Ayodhya's recovery.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Dharma (Rama's continued commitment to his father's command and the path of an ascetic, even if it means foregoing comfort or social interaction.)
Vairagya (Detachment, as Rama chooses a location that fosters greater separation from worldly attachments and the emotional pull of Ayodhya.)
Tapasya (The pursuit of spiritual discipline, for which Rama seeks an undisturbed environment.)
Samadhi (The state of meditative absorption, which is better facilitated in secluded, undisturbed environments, hinting at Rama's intention for deeper spiritual practice.)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: The passage illustrates Rama's commitment to Dharma and Tapasya by deliberately seeking a secluded location for his exile. His choice to move away from Ayodhya, despite the immediate comfort offered by Bharadhvaja, reflects a deep understanding of Vairag – detachment from emotional ties that could hinder his spiritual discipline. This decision shows his resolve to fulfill his ascetic vows in an undisturbed environment conducive to deeper contemplation.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, Rama demonstrates strong emotional regulation and proactive stress management. He wisely recognizes that staying too close to Ayodhya would invite emotional distractions ('people will be tempted to visit us often') and hinder his ability to fully embrace his exile. By choosing a more remote location, he sets healthy boundaries, effectively managing the relationship challenges of separation and prioritizing a stable environment for his own mental and spiritual well-being, as well as the healing of his people back in Ayodhya.
